chapters.category: Ethiopic textual tradition • Modern English research translation
chapters.title: Chapter 56 — The Invasion and the Pit of Sheol
chapters.sourceNote: Translated afresh into clear modern English from the earliest complete primary-language text responsibly available for this chapter. No extant Aramaic or Greek wording has been identified for the Parables. The complete Ethiopic (Geʽez) text in August Dillmann's 1851 critical edition, Liber Henoch Aethiopice, is the translation base for all eight verses, including the angels' iron and bronze chains, the stirring of the Parthian and Median kings, their assault on the land of the Chosen One, their self-destruction, and Sheol's swallowing of the sinners. The difficult reference to the rulers' own chosen and beloved people in verses 3–4 and the transmitted geographical names are retained without conjectural additions. No unattested wording was supplied, and no modern English translation was used as the translation base.

verses.text: There I saw the hosts of the angels of punishment going forth, holding chains of iron and bronze.
verses.study: The vision moves from the judgment of Azazel to another company appointed for punishment. The chains show that the coming military upheaval remains bounded by heavenly judgment rather than uncontrolled fate.
crossReferences: Psalm 149:8–9 — kings and nobles are bound with iron chains
2 Peter 2:4 — rebellious powers are kept in bonds for judgment
Revelation 20:1–3 — a heavenly angel carries a great chain to restrain the deceiver

verses.text: I asked the angel of peace who went with me, saying, ‘For whom are these chains being carried?’
verses.study: Enoch again asks his peaceful guide to interpret instruments of judgment. The question prepares the disclosure that powerful rulers and the people they favor will be unable to escape accountability.
crossReferences: Zechariah 1:9 — the interpreting angel answers the prophet's question
Daniel 8:13 — a heavenly question clarifies the scope of a judgment
Revelation 17:7 — a heavenly guide explains the fate of oppressive power

verses.text: He said to me, ‘They are being carried for their chosen ones and their beloved ones, so that they may be cast into the chasm of the valley's abyss.’
verses.study: The rulers' favored circle shares the rulers' end because it shares their violent error. The chains are carried toward the abyss, where privilege can no longer shield those joined to oppressive power.
crossReferences: Isaiah 24:21–22 — rulers are gathered as prisoners into a pit
Psalm 94:20–23 — rulers allied with wrongdoing are brought to destruction
Revelation 19:19–21 — rulers and their assembled forces meet a common judgment

verses.text: Then that valley will be filled with their chosen and beloved ones. The days of their life will come to an end, and from that time the days of their error will no longer be counted.
verses.study: The valley becomes full, and the long season in which deception appeared to prosper reaches its fixed conclusion. Both life and the continuing tally of error are brought to an appointed end.
crossReferences: Psalm 37:9–10 — the apparent season of the wicked comes to an end
Daniel 7:11–12 — oppressive dominion and life are brought to their limit
Revelation 20:10 — the deceiver's work reaches final judgment

verses.text: In those days the angels will assemble and turn their heads toward the east, toward the people of Parthia and Media. They will stir up the kings, and a spirit of unrest will come upon them. They will rouse them from their thrones, and they will come out like lions from their lairs and like hungry wolves among their flocks.
verses.study: The eastern kings rise under an agitation the vision traces beyond ordinary politics. Lion and wolf imagery exposes predatory violence: rulers leave their security to consume lands and peoples as prey.
crossReferences: Jeremiah 50:41–44 — kings from the north advance like a lion from its thicket
Ezekiel 38:10–12 — a ruler is stirred to invade and seize spoil
Habakkuk 1:8 — invading forces are compared to hungry wolves

verses.text: They will go up and tread upon the land of His chosen ones, and the land of His chosen one will become before them a threshing floor and a trampled path.
verses.study: The invasion reaches the land associated with God's chosen people and Chosen One. Its treatment as a threshing floor portrays severe humiliation, but the possessive language also affirms whose land it remains.
crossReferences: Isaiah 41:15 — threshing imagery depicts nations crushed under judgment
Zechariah 14:2 — the nations gather against Jerusalem
Luke 21:24 — Jerusalem is trampled by the nations for an appointed time

verses.text: But the city of my righteous ones will become a barrier to their horses. They will begin to fight among themselves, and their own right hands will grow strong against them. A man will not recognize his companion or his brother, nor a son his father or his mother, until the number of corpses produced by their slaughter cannot be counted. Their punishment will not be in vain.
verses.study: The invaders' unity collapses at the city of the righteous. Their strength turns inward until social bonds fail and the army destroys itself; the immense loss is presented as a real consequence of their violence, not a meaningless accident.
crossReferences: Judges 7:22 — an invading army turns its sword against its companions
2 Chronicles 20:22–23 — hostile forces destroy one another
Zechariah 14:13 — panic causes each person to strike his neighbor

verses.text: In those days Sheol will open its mouth, and they will sink into it. Their destruction will come to an end as Sheol swallows the sinners from before the face of the chosen ones.
verses.study: Sheol opens beneath the violent host and removes the sinners from the chosen ones' presence. The descent reverses the invaders' proud ascent; deliverance comes through judgment that consumes violence and brings its appointed course to an end.
crossReferences: Numbers 16:30–33 — the ground opens and rebels descend alive to Sheol
Psalm 9:15–18 — nations sink into the pit they made while the needy are remembered
Isaiah 5:14 — Sheol enlarges its throat and opens its mouth without limit

explanation.heading: Chapter teaching and context
paragraphs: Chapter 56 unfolds a judgment on predatory imperial power. Angels carry the chains, eastern kings are stirred from their thrones, and the rulers' favored people are destined for the valley they helped fill through error.

Parthia and Media locate the vision's threat in the east. The text does not invite admiration of conquest: the kings are lions and hungry wolves whose advance turns the chosen land into a trampled threshing floor.

The city of the righteous marks the invaders' limit. Their violence folds back upon them, breaking companionship, brotherhood and even family recognition until the force that came to destroy others destroys itself.

Sheol's open mouth completes the reversal. The host that ascended against the chosen ones sinks from their presence, teaching that violent domination has a boundary and that divine judgment can end it without making the righteous its imitators.

crossReferences: Psalm 149:8–9 — chains prepared for rulers
Ezekiel 38:10–12 — rulers stirred to invade the chosen land
Zechariah 14:2, 13 — invasion followed by mutual slaughter
Isaiah 5:14 — Sheol opens its mouth
Revelation 19:19–21 — assembled rulers and armies brought to judgment
